title: Hosting evaluation and unit economics — SparrowPoint discovery
summary: Introductory discovery focused on per-token unit economics across hosted, dedicated, and private deployment options. Customer is cost-sensitive, needs predictable monthly burn for a Q1 pilot (10M tokens/mo target), and must meet SOC2-ish audit controls, KMS requirements, and VPC networking. Discussed batching/caching levers, quantized model tradeoffs, and possible pilot scope with benchmark runs.

Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS/HSM, audit logs
Next steps: pricing sheet, security docs, benchmark run

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-02
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes (recording truncated at 00:54)
Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez (Redwood); Ellen Park, Ravi Menon, Dana Li (SparrowPoint)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery. Focus on cost per token, how batching and KV cache reduce unit cost, and tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated and fully private installs. Customer wants a predictable monthly budget for a Q1 pilot, plus enterprise security alignment.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:05] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for making time, I see Ellen, Ravi, Dana, good to meet you all. We're Redwood Inference — I'll kick off with a short intro then Diego will peel into the performance and cost levers.
[00:00:18] Ellen Park: Thanks, Maya. Quick note — we're trying to nail down per-token cost for a pilot. We're aiming at roughly 10 million tokens a month to start, potentially spiking to 50M if usage picks up. Key constraints: predictable monthly spend, SOC2 controls, and we may need VPC-only traffic flow.
[00:00:35] Diego Alvarez: Great. I'll cover hosted vs dedicated vs private and then go through batching, caching and quantization impacts. Really important: the per-token numbers are a combination of model efficiency, runtime overhead, and your request patterns.
[00:00:50] Ravi Menon: When you say runtime overhead what's in that, Diego? Is that about GPU hours or something else?
[00:00:58] Diego Alvarez: Good question. It’s a mix: GPU amortized cost per token (which depends on batching), network and serialization, KV cache hits (which avoid re-computing prefixes), and fixed control-plane costs for hosted. For dedicated, you get more predictable GPU amortization because capacity is reserved.
[00:01:15] Maya Chen: To frame it, hosted is our quickest to go-live and easiest to forecast with per-token pricing; dedicated gives you reserved capacity and lower unit cost when you hit committed throughput; private brings the most control for security but usually higher ops overhead.
[00:01:29] Ellen Park: Our procurement person is here — Dana — she cares about contract terms, SLAs, and what would cause cost overruns.
[00:01:36] Dana Li: Hi. Also curious on how burst capacity works, like if we commit to a Dedicated pool for baseline but need extra during launches. How are those bursts priced?
[00:01:45] Diego Alvarez: We usually model burst as either short-term excess capacity billed at a higher per-GPU rate or use mix of hosted fallback. For example, you commit to a Dedicated pool at X GPUs; during burst we can route overflow to hosted endpoints at market per-token rates, with guarded fallback policies so you can control cost vs latency.
[00:02:05] Ellen Park: That hosted fallback — would data leave our VPC in that scenario? That's a no for us if it's PII.
[00:02:10] Diego Alvarez: Right, for private/VPC deployments the fallback can be restricted. We can do strict routing policies where overflow is rejected or queued rather than hitting hosted endpoints. If you want hosted fallback you'd need to opt-in and sign off on data residency allowances.
[00:02:25] Ravi Menon: For our SREs, the quantization stuff is interesting — we've heard lower precision gives big speedups but worries about quality drift. Any rule of thumb?
[00:02:34] Diego Alvarez: Rule of thumb: 4-bit quantization often reduces memory and can improve throughput significantly, but for certain instruction-heavy prompts you might see quality delta. We recommend a quick eval on your prompt set — many customers do a pilot comparing FP16, 8-bit, and 4-bit on key prompts. That’s part of the benchmark plan.
[00:02:50] Maya Chen: And batching: if your request profile has many short requests, batching can either increase latency a bit or you can use continuous micro-batching to keep latency low while improving throughput. The per-token cost improvement depends on average tokens per request and concurrency.
[00:03:05] Ellen Park: Our main application is a summarization microservice — requests are typically 180–400 tokens input and ~120 output. Concurrency is modest — peak 30 rps during working hours.
[00:03:16] Diego Alvarez: Ok that helps. With that profile, KV/prefix caching can be effective if many requests share common prefixes — for summarization that's less likely unless you have templates. But batching will help; with 30 rps and micro-batching we can reach decent GPU utilization and lower per-token cost.
[00:03:33] Dana Li: Can you give a ballpark per-token cost for hosted vs dedicated for a model like the one you're recommending? We understand it's variable but need ranges for procurement.
[00:03:42] Maya Chen: Ballpark—assuming a medium-sized open model and moderate batching: hosted per-token might be $0.0008–$0.002 depending on model size and streaming vs non-streaming. Dedicated committed capacity could drop effective per-token to $0.0003–$0.001 at scale because GPU amortization spreads out. Private on-prem is usually higher initially because of setup and ops, say $0.0006–$0.0012 once amortized but with large upfront infra. These are illustrative; we'll send detailed pricing.
[00:04:12] Ellen Park: That hosted upper bound seems high for us. Is that for low batching?
[00:04:15] Diego Alvarez: Yes, high end is low-batching, peak-time, heavier models. We can right-size model size and quantize to push numbers down. Also caching helps if you have repeated prompts.
[00:04:26] Ravi Menon: About SLAs — if we go Dedicated, what uptime and latency SLOs do you commit to?
[00:04:31] Maya Chen: Dedicated comes with an SLA-backed uptime target—typically 99.9% or higher depending on contract tier. Latency SLOs are discussed per model and route; we usually instrument p99 and p50 latencies and provide dashboards via Redwood Console.
[00:04:46] Dana Li: Procurement needs to see SOC2 and encryption docs before moving forward. Can you share those?
[00:04:50] Maya Chen: Absolutely. I'll drop SOC2 summary, our KMS integration docs, and our private-deployment security whitepaper after the call.
[00:04:58] Ellen Park: For the pilot: we'd like to model two scenarios — "conservative" 10M tokens/mo and "growth" 50M tokens/mo. We need a budget cap and an alerting mechanism if spend approaches the cap.
[00:05:09] Diego Alvarez: No problem. We can build a pilot plan with budget guardrails — token caps, rate limits, and automated alerts. For Dedicated we can structure a monthly committed spend with soft limits to trigger hosted fallback or request throttling.
[00:05:23] Ravi Menon: On the private side, how does KMS work? We have AWS KMS and HSM for some keys — can you integrate?
[00:05:29] Diego Alvarez: Yes, private deployments support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. We provide guide for key wrapping and audit logging. For hosted, we use envelope encryption and can integrate customer keys via dedicated HSM relationships in certain enterprise plans.
[00:05:44] Ellen Park: Let's talk about measurement. How do you calculate per-token numbers we can use in a P&L? Is there a sample workbook?
[00:05:50] Maya Chen: We will share a pricing workbook. The model in the sheet includes: model compute cost (GPU-hours translated to tokens via measured throughput), networking/egress, control plane per-request fee, and any caching savings modeled as percent CPU avoided. We'll also show sensitivity to batching and quantization.
[00:06:07] Dana Li: Please include a row for the committed-dedicated price with burst at hosted rates so procurement can compare.
post_transcript_notes: Customer emphasized strict data residency; private deployment may be required if pilot surfaces PII. Procurement requested SOC2 docs and explicit burst pricing rows. Redwood AE to deliver pricing workbook and Diego to coordinate benchmark. Customer prefers week-of-12/13 for a hands-on benchmark session.
